```{python}
    go_to(p, "RE", (1.0, T("4i", 1)), "motion", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "R1", (1.0, 0.0), "motion", speed=0.5)
    go_to(p, "L3", (1.0, T("4i", -1)), "motion", speed=0.2)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (1.0, T("9")), "motion", speed=3.3)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (4.7, 0.6), "motion", speed=1.4)
    # after the snap: pass protection and a four-man rush; the walked-up Mike drops to the flat
    p.dropback(2.0)
    for k, end in [("LT", (-1.6, -3.6)), ("LG", (-1.4, -1.6)), ("C", (-1.3, 0.0)), ("RG", (-1.4, 1.6)),
                   ("RT", (-1.6, 3.4)), ("Y", (-1.3, 5.6))]:
        go_to(p, k, end, speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "LE", (-2.4, -4.6), "path", speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "L3", (-0.6, -2.2), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "R1", (-0.4, 0.1), "path", speed=2.4)
    go_to(p, "RE", (-0.6, 2.4), "path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (5.0, 9.6), "path", speed=5.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (7.0, 0.4), "path", speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (6.0, -7.6), "path", speed=3.0)
    for k, r_ in [("H", (6.0, -9.6)), ("Z", (8.0, 15.0)), ("X", (8.0, -15.0))]:
        go_to(p, k, r_, "path", speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.3, 2.1), "path", speed=3.0)
    return p


def shift_marks(fld, play, t, i):
    keys = ["L3", "R1"] + (["RE"] if t > -0.35 else [])
    hands(fld, play, keys, t=t, half=0.57)


P_SHIFT = shift_play()
t0 = min(float(f[0, 0]) for f in P_SHIFT._compile()[0].values())
animation_or_strip([(P_SHIFT, round(t0 + 0.05, 1), ""), (P_SHIFT, round(t0 / 2, 1), ""), (P_SHIFT, 0.0, ""),
                    (P_SHIFT, 1.1, "")],
                   notes=["shows four on the line:\ntwo hands down, two edges",
                          "the shift: the edge slides\ninside, the Mike walks up",
                          "snap: five on the line,\nthree hands down: a tite",
                          "it rushes four; the walked-up\nMike drops to the flat"],
                   rings=(("RE", style.DEFENSE),), lateral=(-11.6, 12.0), window=(-7.6, 12.4),
                   after=shift_marks, width_in=6.0)
```

Why go to that trouble? Because, as [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) explained,
an offensive line decides its blocking before the snap: who is covered, who doubles, who climbs, and,
on a pass, which way the center slides and who picks up which rusher. A front that shifts at the last
moment makes those decisions against the wrong picture. In @fig-same-personnel-two-fronts the line set
its rules against a four-man even front with two linebackers; at the snap it faced a five-man line
with one, and on the pass, the player it had counted as a rusher (the walked-up Mike) was in coverage.
Georgia's defense under Kirby Smart is known for doing exactly this, moving from a 4-2-5 into its mint
front before the snap, without a substitution, by sliding a lineman inside to a 4i and standing up an
end on the short side.[^georgia]

The cost of being multiple is complexity. Every front has its own gap assignments and its own fits, and
every player has to know all of them; a shift that is a beat late leaves a gap empty at the snap. That
is why multiple defenses are built around smart, versatile players (edges who can rush and drop,
linemen who can play a 3 and a 4i) and why they live and die on the communication of the
[green-dot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-green-dot) linebacker who relays the call.

## Dialect: Okie, Eagle, G, and the problem with names

You now know what the fronts *are*. A word about what they are *called*, because front names are the
least standardized vocabulary in football. Every staff has a language, inherited from the coaches who
trained its coaches, and the same word can mean different things in neighbouring buildings. Two names
you will hear are good examples.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dialect
#| fig-cap: "Dialect, drawn against the Okie (left). Middle, the Eagle front as many modern 3-4 playbooks use the word: the ends pinch from the tackles' outside shoulders (5s) to their inside shoulders (4is), which is the same picture Fangio's staffs call tite and Smart's call mint. Right, a G front: one letter in the call moves one man, the nose, off the center onto the guard's inside shoulder (a 2i, G for guard), here toward the tight end. Everyone else is where the Okie put him. Dark dots are hands on the ground; the ringed players are the ones who moved."
DIALECT = [("Okie", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ()),
           ("Eagle (one dialect)", [("LE", "4i", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4i", 1)], ("LE", "RE")),
           ("G: nose on a guard", [("LE", "5", -1), ("NT", "2i", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)], ("NT",))]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
for ax, (ttl, spec, moved) in zip(axes, DIALECT):
    dfn = front(spec, lbs=[("WILL", 4.6, -2.1, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.6, 2.1, "M")],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -5.9, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E")])
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    for k in moved:
        p.highlight(k, color=style.DEFENSE)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-7.6, 7.9), window=(-2.6, 7.0), title=False)
    hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.6, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.5)
plt.show()
```

**The [Eagle front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-eagle-front)** has meant at least three things.
In the 1940s it was Greasy Neale's five-man line, the Philadelphia Eagles' defense and the 3-4's
ancestor. In the late 1980s Fritz Shurmur, the Los Angeles Rams' defensive coordinator, built a
linebacker-heavy package he called the Eagle, and later wrote a coaching book on it, *The Eagle Five
Linebacker Defense* (1993); in the Rams' 21–7 playoff win over Philadelphia after the 1989 season,
his defense dropped into zone coverage on almost every snap and, by his own account, never
blitzed.[^shurmur] And in many modern 3-4 playbooks, "Eagle" is the Okie with its ends pinched inside to
4is: the middle panel of @fig-dialect, the same alignment other staffs call tite or mint.[^eaglemodern]
Three meanings, one word, and only context tells you which.

<!-- VERIFY: Shurmur's late-1980s Rams "Eagle" package personnel (sources describe five linebackers; exact count of down linemen varies by account), and the "never blitzed" claim from the UPI recap of the 1989 NFC wild-card game (Rams 21, Eagles 7). -->

**The [G front](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-g-front)** is a tag rather than a whole front: it
moves the nose from the center (or from his shade on the center, in a four-man front) onto a guard's
inside shoulder, a 2i. "G" is for guard. It is a small move with a specific purpose: it forces the
center to step sideways to block the nose, which slows down the center-guard double team on inside zone
and gives the linebacker behind the nose a cleaner path. You'll most often see the G tag on four-man
Over and Under fronts, where it moves a 1-technique to a 2i; the right panel of @fig-dialect applies the
same idea to the Okie.[^gfront]

<!-- VERIFY: whether "G" tags on three-man (Okie) fronts are common usage; the cited source describes G on four-down Over/Under fronts (nose from a 1 to a 2i). -->

The point is not to memorize every staff's dictionary. It is to read the *alignment* first and attach
the name second. If an analyst says "Eagle" and you see 4is inside the tackles, you know what he means
even if his playbook and yours disagree.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, the defensive playbook is a menu of named fronts: pick "3-4 Odd" or "Nickel 3-3-5 Wide" and
the players run to their spots. Real defenses don't call a front from a menu so much as build it from
rules. The call names a front, a tag or two (a G, a slant, who is the edge), and a coverage, and each
player's alignment then depends on where the offense puts its tight end and its back, which side is the
wide side of the field, and whether the offense shifts. Two teams can call the same word and line up
differently, and the same team can call two different words and end up in the same alignment. The
names are shorthand for a set of instructions, and every staff writes its own.
:::

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Houston Texans 2011–2012"}
**The scheme:** Wade Phillips's one-gap 3-4, in his first two seasons as the Texans' defensive
coordinator. The 2011 team's preview called it "his one-gap scheme," and in 2012 its 5-technique end,
J.J. Watt, led the NFL with 20.5 sacks and was Defensive Player of the Year.[^watt]

**What to notice:**

- The ends' alignment and first step. Watt lines up on a tackle's outside shoulder, like an Okie end,
  and then attacks the gap at the snap instead of controlling the man. Count how often his first step is
  across the line.
- What the outside linebackers do. On most passing downs, both are rushing; Phillips's 3-4 rushed four
  like any four-man front.
- How often the "3-4" looks like an Under front with a linebacker standing up. That is the one-gap 3-4
  of @fig-okie-two-ways in its natural habitat.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Denver Broncos, Super Bowl 50 (2015 season)"}
**The game:** Super Bowl 50, February 7, 2016, at Levi's Stadium: Denver 24, Carolina 10. Phillips,
now Denver's coordinator, had the league's top defense by yards allowed, and in the Super Bowl his two
stand-up edges, Von Miller and DeMarcus Ware, chased the league MVP, Cam Newton, all night. Miller was
the game's MVP, with 2.5 sacks and two forced fumbles, one of which set up Denver's first
touchdown.[^sb50]

**What to notice:** the edges. Before each snap, find Miller and Ware: standing, wide, often on
different sides from snap to snap. Watch whether they rush or drop (mostly rush), how they win around
the tackles with speed, and how, on Newton's scrambles and designed runs, they keep contain rather than
racing past him. The stand-up edge as a weapon is this game.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2024"}
**The season:** Vic Fangio's first year as the Eagles' defensive coordinator. The defense allowed the
fewest yards in the NFL, about 278 a game, and the season ended with a 40–22 Super Bowl LIX win in which
the Eagles pressured Patrick Mahomes with four-man rushes.[^eagles24] Its five-man front was the tite of
this chapter, with Jordan Davis, a 341-pound nose at his combine, between two 4is, usually Jalen Carter
and Milton Williams, and two edges outside them.[^eaglesfront]

**What to notice:**

- Count the hands down on early downs. Three inside the tackles, with an edge on each side, is the tite.
- Watch Davis against a double team on an inside run: does the pair move him? Then find the linebacker
  behind him and see whether a blocker ever reaches him.
- Watch the safeties on those runs. They start deep, often 12 yards or more, and arrive late but fast.
  That is the light-box bargain: the front holds the line so the safeties can stay home on the pass.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Georgia 2021"}
**The season:** Kirby Smart's Georgia defense, which many observers rank among the best in college
football history, won the national championship, beating Alabama 33–18.[^georgia] Its front featured two
interior linemen the Eagles later drafted in the first round, Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter, so the 2021
Bulldogs and the 2024 Eagles are, in a sense, the same front four years apart.

**What to notice:** the pre-snap movement. Georgia often lines up in a four-man front and shifts into
its mint front, a tackle sliding inside to a 4i and a defensive end standing up, as the offense calls
its plays. Watch the offensive line's heads turn as the front changes, and then where the run goes.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap: count the hands, find the center.**

- Is anybody head-up on the center? A nose over the ball means an odd front; nobody there means an even
  one.
- Count the hands on the ground. Four is a four-man line, whatever the graphic says. Two down plus two
  standing edges is also a four-man line, usually a 3-4 team's 2-4-5 nickel. Three inside the tackles
  plus a standing edge on each side is a five-man tite (or mint) front.
- Who is standing on the edges? A standing edge is a rusher who might drop; note his number and watch
  him on passes.
- Where are the ends: outside the tackles (5s, built to beat the reach and set the edge), head-up (4s, two-gappers)
  or inside them (4is, a tite, built to choke inside runs)?

**At the snap: the first step and the count.**

- Did the front change in the last seconds? A shift (an edge sliding inside, a linebacker walking up)
  means the defense is trying to beat the offensive line's blocking calls.
- Do the ends step into the tackles' chests (two-gap) or into the gaps (one-gap)?
- On a pass, how many rushed, and who? Five on the line rushing four means somebody standing at the line
  dropped.

**After the play: where did the run go?**

- Against a tite, did the inside run get through, or did it bounce outside? If it bounced, who made the
  tackle: an edge, the linebacker, or a safety?
- Did the offense's play fit the front? Inside zone into a tite is a fight on the defense's terms;
  outside zone and perimeter runs test its edges.

For your prediction log ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on first and second down, write down the number of hands on the ground and whether the front was odd or
even, then whether the run went inside or outside. After a quarter you'll know which front the defense
uses to stop what, and whether the offense noticed.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1. Name it, then pick a run.** First-and-10 from the offense's own 35. The offense is in the
shotgun with three receivers and an attached tight end (Y). The defense is in nickel. Name the front.
How many defenders are in the box, and how many blockers does the offense have? If you were calling the
run, would you run inside zone, or something else?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: the defense's alignment before the snap (dark dots are hands on the ground). Two safeties deep, a nickel ($) over the slot on the left, and the corners on the wide receivers (outside the picture)."
off = gun11(y_attached=True)
dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
       D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E"),
       D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")] + secondary(nickel_w=-6.2, high=11.5, safety_w=7.6)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: first-and-10, nickel")
f = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-12.2, 12.2), window=(-7.4, 13.6))
hands(f, p, ("L4", "NT", "R4"))
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A tite front in nickel: a 3-3-5 by the count.** Three hands down inside the tackles (a 4i, a 0 and a
4i) with a stand-up edge on each side make five on the line, and one linebacker stands behind them.

**Six in the box against six blockers** (five linemen and the tight end), with two safeties deep and the
nickel outside the box. On paper that is a light box, and analysts will tell you to run against light
boxes. But this light box was *built* to be run into. Inside zone aims at the play-side B gap, where the
4i is; the nose and the 4is will occupy all five offensive linemen, and the Mike will run free, as in
@fig-tite-inside-zone.

**The better calls test what the tite gives up.** Outside zone or a toss to the tight-end side makes the
tight end block a stand-up edge alone and asks the Mike and the strong safety to beat the ball to the
alley. A run with the quarterback reading the backside edge (a zone read) turns the unblocked edge into
a wasted defender. Or don't run at all: a single linebacker in a light box is exactly the defender an
RPO or a quick throw underneath attacks. The defense has dared you to run inside; the smart offense
declines.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2. Choose your front.** You coordinate the defense. This week's opponent runs outside zone more
than any other play, from tight formations with the quarterback under center, and its tight end is an
excellent blocker. Here are two fronts you could show on first down. Which would you rather be in, and
where will the run most likely go against each?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: two fronts against the same under-center, one-tight-end formation. Front A: the tite: a 0 and two 4is between two stand-up edges, the right edge on the tight end's outside shoulder (a 9), one linebacker. Front B: a four-man even front aligned wide: a 3-technique on the right guard's outside shoulder, a 1 on the center, a 5 on the left tackle and a defensive end (9) on the tight end, with two linebackers."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
OFF_UC = line("short") + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
fA = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -5.3, "E"), D("L4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", -1), "4i"), D("NT", "DL", 1.0, 0.0, "0"),
      D("R4", "DL", 1.0, T("4i", 1), "4i"), D("RE", "OLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.7, 0.8, "M")]
fB = front([("LE", "5", -1), ("L1", "1", -1), ("R3", "3", 1), ("RE", "9", 1)],
           lbs=[("WILL", 4.7, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 4.7, 1.6, "M")])
for ax, dfn, hd, ttl in [(axes[0], fA, ("L4", "NT", "R4"), "Front A: tite"),
                         (axes[1], fB, ("LE", "L1", "R3", "RE"), "Front B: wide four-man")]:
    p = Play(OFF_UC, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.8), window=(-8.4, 6.8), title=False)
    hands(f, p, hd)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Front B is the better bet against this opponent, though neither is free.** Outside zone lives on reach
blocks. In Front B, the defenders on the play side are all *outside* the men who must reach them: the 3
outside the right guard, the end outside the tight end. Those are the hardest reaches in football, and a
quick 3-technique can be through the B gap before the guard gets there (the one-gap animation in
[Defensive Line Play](05-01-dl-techniques-and-gap-control.qmd)). If the reaches fail, the back can't get
outside and has to cut up early, into two linebackers.

In Front A, the play-side 4i and the nose are *inside* their blockers, the easiest reaches there are, so
the line can get its heads across and run the defense sideways. Everything then rests on one edge
holding the tight end, an excellent blocker, by himself, with one linebacker and a safety coming from
depth to fill the alley. Expect the ball to bounce outside if the edge is reached, or to cut back if the
Mike over-runs it.

**What Front B gives up:** the interior. Against the same team's *inside* zone, the 1 and the 3 can be
doubled and the doubles can climb to two linebackers. That is why defenses facing an outside-zone team
mix fronts by down and formation instead of living in one, and why the tite's teams widen their edges
(or switch to four-man fronts) against wide-zone offenses.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3. Which 3-4 is it?** Two snaps from the same 3-4 defense against the same formation. The
pictures show the first step of each lineman (orange arrows), a quarter-second after the snap. For each
snap, say whether the front is playing two-gap or one-gap, and which linebackers you expect to be free.

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: two snaps, one quarter-second after the snap (linemen drawn a little deeper than real so their first steps show; dark dots are hands on the ground). Snap A: a nose head-up on the center and ends head-up on the tackles, each stepping straight into the blocker in front of him. Snap B: the nose shaded toward the tight end and the ends on the outside shoulders of the guard and the tackle, each stepping into the gap beside his blocker."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.4))
for ax, snapB in [(axes[0], False), (axes[1], True)]:
    spec = [("LE", "3", -1), ("NT", "1", 1), ("RE", "5", 1)] if snapB else [("LE", "4", -1), ("NT", "0", 1), ("RE", "4", 1)]
    dfn = front(spec, lbs=[("WILL", 5.4, -2.0, "W"), ("MIKE", 5.4, 2.0, "M")],
                others=[("LOLB", 1.0, -5.9, "E"), ("ROLB", 1.0, T("9"), "E")])
    dfn = [q.moved(d=2.1) if q.key in ("LE", "NT", "RE") else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(line("short") + [te(+1)], dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if snapB:
        moves = [("LE", (1.05, -2.55)), ("NT", (1.05, 0.85)), ("RE", (1.05, 4.1))]
    else:
        moves = [("LE", (0.85, -3.2)), ("NT", (0.85, 0.0)), ("RE", (0.85, 3.2))]
    for k, end in moves:
        go_to(p, k, end, "path", speed=3.0)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-8.0, 8.4), window=(-2.6, 7.6), title=False)
    hands(f, p, ("LE", "NT", "RE"))
    ax.set_title("Snap B" if snapB else "Snap A", fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.7)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Snap A is two-gap.** Head-up alignments (a 0 and two 4s) and first steps straight *into* the blockers
are the signature: each lineman is striking the man in front of him, about to lock out and read. That
means three linemen are holding six gaps, the edge on the tight end has the D gap, and **both inside
linebackers are free**: they have no gap of their own at the snap and will read and fill wherever the
ball goes. If the linemen win, nobody blocks either of them.

**Snap B is one-gap.** Shaded alignments (a 3, a 1 and a 5) and first steps *into the gaps* beside the
blockers: the nose into the A gap toward the tight end, the left end into the B gap, the right end into
the C gap. Every lineman has one gap, so the linebackers have one each too: the Mike the B gap toward
the tight end, the Will the other A gap, as in the right half of @fig-okie-two-ways. **Nobody is free**,
but everybody is fast. This is the Under-like 3-4 that Wade Phillips ran for decades.

The lesson is the one this chapter keeps repeating: the roster said 3-4 both times. The alignment and
the first step told you which 3-4.
:::
:::

## Back to the broadcast

The chapter opened with a graphic that said 3-4 and a picture that kept changing. Now you can read both.

- *The graphic says 3-4, and you count four on the line, two standing*: that is the 3-4 team's
  **2-4-5 nickel**, its nose on the bench and its two outside linebackers on the edges. The roster says
  2-4-5; the football is a four-man line. Count hands, not names.
- *Next snap, five across the line, three of them enormous and wedged inside the tackles, one linebacker
  behind them*: a **tite**, built from the same personnel by sliding an edge inside and standing up
  another player at the end of the line. A **multiple** defense, changing fronts without substituting.
- *The inside run into a wall, the linebacker never touched*: the tite's whole purpose. A nose and two 4is
  occupy all five offensive linemen, the doubles can't climb, and the one linebacker makes the tackle.
  That is how six defenders stop a run aimed at six blockers: one of them, the nose, is doing the work of
  two.

## Takeaways

- **Find the center.** A defender head-up on the center makes the front odd; nobody there makes it even.
  The odd fronts are built around a heavy nose who takes two blockers so somebody else can run free.
- **The 3-4 Okie is one alignment played two ways.** Two-gap (head-up, control and read) keeps the inside
  linebackers clean at the cost of rare bodies and little pass rush; one-gap (shaded, attack) turns the
  3-4 into an aggressive front, often an Under with a standing Sam. The first step tells you which.
- **The stand-up edge is the 3-4's great legacy.** Standing gives him vision, width and the option to
  drop, which makes the defense's rush uncertain; the price is leverage against the run.
- **The tite walls off the middle.** A 0 and two 4is cover every interior blocker, so inside zone's double
  teams can neither move them nor climb, and a light box with two safeties deep can still stop inside runs.
  It gives up pass rush, the perimeter and the space underneath.
- **Fronts choose what to stop.** Line up on or inside blockers to beat double teams (inside runs); line up
  outside them to beat reaches (outside zone). No front does both, so defenses change fronts by opponent,
  by situation and by shifting at the snap.
- **Nickel labels are roster labels.** 4-2-5, 2-4-5 and most NFL 3-3-5s describe nearly the same box count
  and pass rush; what differs is whether the edges are listed as ends or linebackers. Count hands, not
  names, and read alignment before dialect.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**Measuring the wall.** The tite's promise is that nobody climbs: every offensive lineman is still engaged
with a defensive lineman a second after the snap, so the linebacker behind them is untouched. Tracking data
can test that. In the simulated tite play above, here is the distance from the Mike to the nearest
offensive lineman at three moments, computed from its Big Data Bowl-format frames (simulated, BDB-format):

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (nearest blocker to the linebacker, from tracking frames)"
def nearest_blocker(play, key, times=(0.5, 1.0, 1.4)):
    trk = play.to_tracking()
    me = trk[trk.displayName == key].set_index("time")
    ol = trk[trk.displayName.isin(OL_KEYS + ("Y",))]
    out = {}
    for t in times:
        m = me.loc[round(t, 1)]
        o = ol[ol.time.round(1) == round(t, 1)]
        out[f"+{t:.1f} s"] = f"{np.hypot(o.x - m.x, o.y - m.y).min():.1f} yd"
    return out


as_markdown(pd.DataFrame([{"defender": "Mike, tite vs inside zone (simulated)", **nearest_blocker(P_TITE, "MIKE")}]))
```

On real frames the same measure, computed for every inside linebacker on every run, separates fronts that
keep linebackers clean from fronts that don't. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9)
has tracking for every player and a players file with positions; pair it with the nflverse participation
data above to tag each snap's front. The data needs a free Kaggle login, so this cell is not run when the
book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
runs = plays[plays["isDropback"] == False]
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
if "position" not in trk:
    trk = trk.merge(players, on="nflId", how="left")

OL = {"T", "G", "C"}
out = []
for g, pl in runs[["gameId", "playId"]].itertuples(index=False):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl, label="position")
    at1 = one[one["time"].round(1) == 1.0]
    lbs, ol = at1[at1["position"].isin(["ILB", "MLB"])], at1[at1["position"].isin(OL)]
    for r in lbs.itertuples():
        out.append({"gameId": g, "playId": pl, "nflId": r.nflId,
                    "nearest_ol": float(np.hypot(ol.x - r.x, ol.y - r.y).min())})
clean = pd.DataFrame(out)
(clean.nearest_ol > 2.0).mean()   # share of inside-linebacker run snaps with no blocker within 2 yards at 1 s
```
